To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) for any constant $\gamma > 2/3$, BPP algorithms can be efficiently simulated using a very weak random \ds, and (2) for any constant $c > 0$, there is a BPP algorithm that runs in polynomial time using a very weak \ds\ of min-entropy rate $R^c$.

(i) the output of any weak random source of min-entropy rate $\gamma > 5/6$ can be used to simulate any randomized algorithm in time $n^\gamma$; (ii) the output of a Chor--Goldreic\ source of min- entropy rate $\gamma >1/2$ can be used for a polynomial time simulation.
\begin{itemize}\item For any $\gamma > 2/3$, one can run BPP algorithms using a very weak source with min-entropy rate $\gamma$.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how much randomness is needed in a randomized algorithm to obtain a given level of error.
the following fundamental problem: How many truly random bits are necessary to run a randomized algorithm using a very weak random number generator as a source of randomness?
the following questions: (i) What is the minimal amount of entropy needed to simulate a given probabilistic algorithm? (ii) How can we extract randomness from a source that has very little entropy?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we show that the hardness of approximations is equivalent to the hardness of extracting randomness from weak sources of randomness.
we show how to run randomized algorithms in polynomial time using a source of min-entropy rate $R^\gamma$ for any constant $\gamma > 2/3$.
we can run randomized algorithms in polynomial time using weak random sources of entropy rate well below constant.

we show how to run randomized algorithms using a weak random source, and that the running time is polynomially related to the min-entropy rate of the source.

we show how to efficiently extract randomness from a \ds\ using a very small number of truly random bits; this can be used to simulate randomized algorithms in time $O(n^{O(\log k n)})$ using a weak random source of min-entropy $(R^{\Omega(k)})$.
The main takeaway from our work is that
randomness extraction is a powerful tool for derandomization.
weak sources of min-entropies $R^\gamma$, for $\gamma > \frac12$, are not significantly weaker than truly random sources.
randomness can be extracted efficiently from very weak random sources.
